chunks: Abdullah ibn Kaysan informed me, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).
He said: I said to him, 'May I be made your ransom, I am your devotee Abdullah ibn Kaysan.' He said: 'As for the lineage, I recognise it; but as for you, I do not recognise you.'

He said: I said to him, 'I was born in the mountains and grew up in the land of Persia. I mix with people in business and other matters. I come across a man and see in him good conduct, good morals, and abundant trustworthiness — then I investigate and find him to be an enemy of yours. And I come across a man and see from him evil morals, little trustworthiness, and malice — then I investigate and find him to be one of your followers. How can this be?'

Then he said to me: 'Did you not know, O son of Kaysan, that God, Mighty and Majestic, took a clay from Paradise and a clay from the Fire, then mixed them both together, then separated this from that and that from this? So what you saw in those ones — the trustworthiness, good morals, and good conduct — is from what the clay of Paradise touched them with, and they will return to what they were created from. And what you saw in these ones — the little trustworthiness, evil morals, and malice — is from what the clay of the Fire touched them with, and they will return to what they were created from.'

key_terms.السمت: Conduct/demeanor — outward appearance, bearing, and manner of behavior in public
key_terms.العداوة: Enmity — opposition to and rejection of the authority of the Imams
key_terms.الولاية: Wilayah — allegiance and devotion to the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt
key_terms.زعارّة: Malice/meanness — a rare Quranic/classical word for moral baseness, corruption, or aggressiveness
key_terms.طينة: Clay/essence — in Shia cosmology, the primordial substance from which each person's soul-essence was created, determining their spiritual orientation

ai.seo_question: Why do some enemies of the Imams have good morals while some followers have bad morals in Shia theology?
ai.summary: In this narration, a companion named Abdullah ibn Kaysan presents a puzzling observation to Imam al-Sadiq (AS): enemies of the Imams sometimes display exemplary character, while followers sometimes exhibit moral failings. The Imam resolves the paradox through a cosmological doctrine: God took clay from both Paradise and the Fire, mixed them, then separated them. Every human being carries a trace of both clays, and the dominant clay determines their eventual destiny — believers bear the imprint of paradise clay and will return to it, disbelievers bear the imprint of fire clay and will return to it. This doctrine, known in Shia theology as the doctrine of 'tina' (clay/essence), explains why external morality does not alone determine a person's inner nature or eschatological fate.
